concept.name: Hinted Handoff & Repair

relationships.description: Connects Hinted Handoff & Repair to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Hinted handoff buffers writes on healthy coordinator nodes when a target replica is temporarily unreachable, while read repair and anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair reconcile silent divergence over time.
spark.keyTakeaway: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.

concept.whyItMatters: In leaderless or dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak, DynamoDB-style quorums), nodes restart, suffer GC pauses, or experience transient network partitions daily. Without hinted handoff, a single downed replica drops write availability for consistency levels like ANY or forces coordinators to fail writes; without read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy, replicas permanently drift out of sync and resurrected nodes can serve stale values or reintroduce deleted rows (tombstone zombies).
whenToUse: High-availability AP/tunable-consistency clusters (e.g., Cassandra with RF=3, CL=LOCAL_ONE or LOCAL_QUORUM) where brief node restarts (5–30 minutes) must not stall writes.
Geo-distributed or multi-AZ deployments experiencing transient cross-AZ packet loss where coordinators can buffer hints locally until peers recover.
Workloads with skewed read/write ratios where background anti-entropy (nodetool repair) and probabilistic read repair close consistency gaps without blocking the write path.
whenNotToUse: Strictly linearizable systems (e.g., etcd/Raft or Spanner Paxos) where unacknowledged writes to a minority cannot be buffered as hints on non-owning nodes without violating consensus.
Extended replica outages exceeding max_hint_window_in_ms (typically 3 hours in Cassandra); storing hints longer risks coordinator disk exhaustion and replay storms.
Write-heavy workloads running near coordinator disk IOPS or heap limits, where hint serialization and replay compete directly with live mutations.
keyPoints: Hints are stored on the coordinator (or a designated proxy) as (target_host_id, mutation, timestamp) and are NOT counted toward quorum acknowledgments like LOCAL_QUORUM—only ConsistencyLevel.ANY counts a hint as a successful write.
Bounded hint windows (e.g., Cassandra's max_hint_window_in_ms = 10800000 ms / 3 hours) prevent unbounded disk growth when a node is permanently dead rather than transiently flapping.
Read repair runs synchronously (blocking on digest mismatches when CL > ONE) or asynchronously in the background, reconciling only the specific keys that are actively read.

Anti-entropy repair uses Merkle trees—hierarchical cryptographic hashes over token ranges—to pinpoint divergent sub-ranges between replicas in O(log N) tree traversal without streaming entire SSTables.

Tombstone retention (gc_grace_seconds, default 10 days in Cassandra) must exceed the anti-entropy repair interval; otherwise a down node can miss a delete tombstone and resurrect deleted data upon recovery.

examples.title: Rolling Kernel Patch on a 12-Node Cassandra Cluster
examples.scenario: An SRE team performs a rolling OS patch across 12 Cassandra nodes (RF=3, writes at LOCAL_QUORUM). Each node is drained and rebooted for 8 minutes. During each 8-minute window, coordinators buffer mutations destined for the rebooting node in /var/lib/cassandra/hints at ~4,500 hints/sec (~2.16M hints total per node reboot).
examples.outcome: Writes continue with zero client errors at p99 = 6.2 ms. Once the patched node rejoins via Gossip, coordinators throttle hint replay at hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (1024 KB/s per node), draining the 8-minute backlog in ~11 minutes without triggering full-range Merkle-tree repairs.

examples.title: Silent Bit-Rot and Cold-Key Divergence Resolved by Incremental Repair
examples.scenario: A ScyllaDB cluster stores 40 TB of IoT telemetry where 70% of partitions are write-once and rarely read after 24 hours. A network switch flap drops 0.4% of async replica writes over 6 hours—too brief to trip alerts, and cold keys never trigger read repair.
examples.outcome: Weekly incremental anti-entropy repair exchanges 32-level Merkle trees per vnode token range, isolating the 160 GB of divergent sub-ranges and streaming only the mismatched SSTable blocks rather than transferring all 40 TB.

tradeOffs.factor: Write Availability vs. Coordinator Disk & Replay Pressure
tradeOffs.pro: Coordinators absorb mutations during transient peer outages, keeping write success rates near 100% even when a replica is down.
tradeOffs.con: Hints consume local coordinator disk, JVM/memory buffers, and network bandwidth during replay, risking cascading latency spikes when multiple nodes recover simultaneously.

tradeOffs.factor: Read Repair vs. Read Tail Latency
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronously repairs hot keys on the fly when CL >= QUORUM, keeping frequently accessed records convergent without waiting for scheduled repairs.
tradeOffs.con: Requires digest requests to all replicas (or R+1) and extra round-trips on mismatch, inflating p99 read latency by 1.5x–3x during replica divergence.

tradeOffs.factor: Full Merkle-Tree Repair vs. Cluster CPU/I/O Overhead
tradeOffs.pro: Guarantees eventual consistency even for cold, never-read keys and ensures tombstones propagate before gc_grace_seconds expires.
tradeOffs.con: Building Merkle trees requires full SSTable scans and compaction/streaming I/O; poorly throttled repairs can double disk utilization and starve foreground queries.

failureModes.name: Hint Replay Storm
failureModes.description: A node returns after a 2.5-hour outage while 20 coordinators each hold gigabytes of queued hints. Unthrottled parallel replay saturates the recovering node's NIC, memtables, and compaction threads, causing it to fail health checks and flap.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap max_hint_window_in_ms (e.g., 1–3 hours), enforce hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (e.g., 1024 KB/s divided across active peers), and pause hint delivery if the target's pending compaction queue exceeds threshold.

failureModes.name: Zombie Data Resurrection
failureModes.description: A replica stays offline longer than gc_grace_seconds (e.g., 10 days). Healthy replicas purge expired delete tombstones via compaction. When the offline node returns—or a stale hint arrives—the pre-delete value reappears because the tombstone is gone.
failureModes.mitigation: Run anti-entropy repair strictly within gc_grace_seconds (e.g., every 3–5 days for a 10-day grace period), and never re-add a node that has been down longer than gc_grace_seconds without wiping and bootstrapping it fresh.

failureModes.name: Hint Disk Exhaustion on Coordinators
failureModes.description: During a prolonged AZ isolation, coordinators accumulate hints for an entire unreachable rack until /var/lib/cassandra/hints fills the root or data volume, crashing healthy coordinators.
failureModes.mitigation: Mount hints on a dedicated volume or enforce max_hints_file_size_in_mb and total hint disk caps; disable hinted handoff for cross-DC links when WAN links are saturated.

failureModes.name: Merkle-Tree Over-Streaming (Coarse Granularity)
failureModes.description: With a fixed-depth Merkle tree (e.g., depth 15 = 32,768 leaves) over a multi-terabyte token range, a single divergent key forces streaming an entire leaf bucket of tens of megabytes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use virtual nodes (vnodes) or sub-range repair (e.g., Cassandra Reaper) to keep per-repair token ranges small, and enable incremental repair so already-repaired SSTables are excluded from future tree builds.

commonMistakes: Assuming hinted handoff satisfies LOCAL_QUORUM—hints do NOT count as quorum acks; only ConsistencyLevel.ANY accepts a hint as a write success.
Disabling scheduled nodetool repair because hinted handoff and read repair are enabled, leaving cold keys permanently inconsistent and tombstones unpropagated.
Setting gc_grace_seconds shorter than the actual repair cycle, guaranteeing deleted records will resurrect as zombies after a node outage.
Running full-cluster repairs simultaneously on all nodes instead of staggering sub-range repairs with tools like Cassandra Reaper, triggering cluster-wide compaction storms.
Replacing a dead node with a new node using the same IP without running `nodetool assassinate` or proper bootstrap, causing coordinators to replay stale hints onto an empty ring slot.

sections.content:
## The idea

Distributed databases without a single leader (Dynamo, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak) decouple write availability from strict replica liveness. When a client writes a key with replication factor `RF=3`, the coordinator routes the mutation to all three owning replicas in parallel. If Replica C is temporarily unreachable—due to a 90-second GC pause, a rolling restart, or a top-of-rack switch flap—the coordinator cannot immediately deliver the mutation to C.

**Hinted handoff** solves the short-term gap: the coordinator writes a *hint* to its own local disk containing the target node's UUID, the mutation payload, and the original write timestamp. Once Gossip signals that Replica C is back online, the coordinator streams the queued hints to C in the background. Crucially, hinted handoff is a best-effort optimization for transient outages, not a durability guarantee: if the coordinator itself dies before replaying the hint, or if Replica C stays down past `max_hint_window_in_ms` (default 3 hours), the hint is dropped.

**Read repair** and **anti-entropy repair** close the remaining consistency gaps. Read repair compares data or SHA-256/MD5 digests across replicas during live reads and patches stale replicas with the newest timestamped value. Anti-entropy repair runs offline on a schedule, building **Merkle trees** over token ranges so replicas exchange compact tree hashes and stream only the mismatched key ranges—ensuring even cold, never-read data converges and delete tombstones propagate before `gc_grace_seconds` expires.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a 6-node Cassandra cluster (`RF=3`, `CL=LOCAL_QUORUM`, `max_hint_window_in_ms=10800000`) handling an e-commerce inventory update `UPDATE stock SET qty = 42 WHERE sku = 'SKU-901'` at timestamp `t = 1731430000000000` (microseconds).

1. **Write & Hint Capture**: The client sends the write to Coordinator `N1`. Consistent hashing maps `'SKU-901'` to replicas `N2`, `N4`, and `N5`. `N2` and `N4` acknowledge within 2.1 ms, satisfying `LOCAL_QUORUM` (2 of 3). `N5` is rebooting, so its TCP socket refuses connections. Because `N5` has been down for less than 3 hours, `N1` appends the mutation to `/var/lib/cassandra/hints/N5-uuid-1731430000.hints` and returns `200 OK` to the client.
2. **Hint Replay on Recovery**: Four minutes later, `N5` finishes rebooting and announces `STATUS=NORMAL` via Gossip. `N1` detects the state transition, opens its hint file for `N5`, and streams the buffered mutations at `1024 KB/s`. `N5` applies the write using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) timestamp `1731430000000000`, and `N1` deletes the hint segment once acknowledged.
3. **Read Repair on Mismatch**: Suppose a second write `qty = 41` at `t + 5s` suffered a dropped packet to `N4` while `N1`'s hint buffer was briefly disabled. Later, a client reads `'SKU-901'` at `LOCAL_QUORUM`: `N1` requests the full row from `N2` and a 32-byte digest from `N4`. The digests mismatch (`N2` has `qty=41`, `N4` has `qty=42`). `N1` fetches the full row from `N4`, resolves LWW (`t + 5s` wins), returns `qty=41` to the client, and issues a blocking read-repair mutation to `N4`.
4. **Anti-Entropy Merkle Repair**: Every 4 days (well inside the 10-day `gc_grace_seconds`), Cassandra Reaper triggers an incremental repair on token range `[0x4000, 0x4FFF]`. `N2`, `N4`, and `N5` each compute a depth-15 Merkle tree over unrepaired SSTables in that range (~1 MB each), exchange the root and branch hashes, find 3 divergent leaf buckets out of 32,768, and stream only those ~18 MB of missing rows.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / How hinted handoff, read repair, and Merkle repair complement each other
sections.content:
## How hinted handoff, read repair, and Merkle repair complement each other

No single repair mechanism is sufficient on its own in an AP/tunable-consistency store:

- **Hinted handoff** is *write-triggered* and *push-based*. It has near-zero impact on read latency and handles 95%+ of routine rolling restarts and brief network blips. However, it fails if the coordinator crashes before replay or if the outage outlives `max_hint_window_in_ms`.
- **Read repair** is *read-triggered* and *lazy*. Using digest requests (comparing hashes rather than full payloads across replicas), it catches divergence on hot keys without scheduling overhead. Yet cold keys—such as archived orders or historical logs—are never read and therefore never repaired by read repair.
- **Anti-entropy repair** is *schedule-triggered* and *exhaustive*. By hashing token sub-ranges into Merkle trees, replicas detect every divergent key—hot or cold—including missing delete tombstones. Its cost is background disk I/O and network streaming, which is why modern deployments use **incremental repair** (marking already-repaired SSTables) and **sub-range orchestration** (splitting a 256-vnode ring into thousands of small tasks) to bound cluster impact.

## Repair mechanism comparison

| Mechanism | Trigger | Scope | Latency Impact | Primary Failure Gap |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hinted Handoff** | Write fails to reach a replica | Missed writes within `max_hint_window` (e.g., 3h) | Adds coordinator disk append (~0.2 ms); zero read impact | Lost if coordinator dies or outage > hint window |
| **Blocking Read Repair** | Read digest mismatch (`CL > ONE`) | Actively read keys only | Inflates p99 read latency (extra RTT + mutation) | Never repairs cold, unread keys |
| **Background Read Repair** | Probabilistic or async mismatch | Actively read keys only | None on foreground read response | Eventual only; can lag under high load |
| **Full / Incremental Merkle Repair** | Scheduled cron / Reaper (every 3–7d) | Entire token range (hot + cold + tombstones) | High background CPU, disk scan, and streaming I/O | Can cause compaction storms if unthrottled |

## Failure modes

- **Tombstone resurrection (Zombie data)**: If a node is offline for 12 days while `gc_grace_seconds` is 10 days (864,000 s), healthy nodes compact away delete tombstones on Day 11. When the offline node returns on Day 12, its pre-delete SSTables still hold the deleted row—and anti-entropy repair treats that row as *missing* on the healthy nodes, propagating the deleted data back across the entire cluster.
- **Hint replay storm & GC/compaction collapse**: When a node recovers after 2.9 hours of downtime in a 10,000 writes/sec cluster, 20 coordinators may simultaneously flush ~5 GB of hints. Without `hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb`, the recovering node's memtables flush thousands of tiny SSTables, triggering an L0 compaction backlog and OOMs.
- **Coordinator disk saturation**: Storing hints on the same NVMe volume as live SSTables means a multi-hour rack outage can fill the disk to 100%, halting all writes on healthy coordinators.
- **Merkle-tree validation memory spikes**: Computing deep Merkle trees across wide partitions or uncompacted SSTables allocates significant off-heap/heap buffers and random IOPS, degrading foreground p99 latency.

## Tuning parameters & operational math

Three formulas govern safe operation in Cassandra/ScyllaDB-class systems:

1. **Hint Disk Budget**: `Peak_Hint_Bytes = Write_Rate_Bytes_Per_Sec * (RF - 1) * Outage_Hours * 3600 / Healthy_Coordinators`. At 20 MB/s cluster ingest (`RF=3`) and 1 downed node out of 12 for 3 hours, coordinators accumulate `~39 GB` per coordinator (~470 GB total) if all writes miss that replica—requiring explicit `max_hints_directory_size` caps.
2. **Replay Drain Time**: `Drain_Seconds = Total_Hint_KB / (Throttle_KB_Per_Sec * Active_Coordinators_Targeting_Node)`. Remember Cassandra's `hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb` is divided by the number of *all* nodes in the cluster or per-coordinator depending on version—verify throughput via `nodetool netstats`.
3. **Tombstone Safety Invariant**: Always enforce `Repair_Cycle + Max_Repair_Duration + Outage_Detection_Buffer < gc_grace_seconds`. With `gc_grace_seconds = 864000` (10 days), target a complete incremental repair every 3–4 days.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Set `max_hint_window_in_ms` to 3 hours (10800000 ms) or less; never rely on hints for multi-day outages.
- [ ] Place `/var/lib/cassandra/hints` on a dedicated volume or configure a hard disk-space cap so hints cannot starve SSTables.
- [ ] Schedule automated sub-range incremental repairs (e.g., Cassandra Reaper) to complete every 3–5 days, strictly below `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days).
- [ ] Throttle hint replay (`hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb`) and repair streaming (`stream_throughput_outbound_megabits_per_sec`) based on 30% of available NIC/disk headroom.
- [ ] Monitor `HintedHandoff` pending counts, `ReadRepair` rates, and `Compaction` pending tasks; alert if any repair cycle misses its `gc_grace_seconds` deadline.
- [ ] Wipe and re-bootstrap any node that has been offline longer than `gc_grace_seconds` instead of rejoining it directly.

interviewProblems.title: Hinted Handoff & Repair
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Hinted Handoff & Repair. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Hinted handoff buffers writes on healthy coordinator nodes when a target replica is temporarily unreachable, while read repair and anti-entropy Merkle-tree repair reconcile silent divergence over time.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Replicas N2 & N4 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Replica N5.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Replica N5 experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap max_hint_window_in_ms (e.g., 1–3 hours), enforce hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (e.g., 1024 KB/s divided across active peers), and pause hint delivery if the target's pending compaction queue exceeds threshold.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.
Avoid trap: Assuming hinted handoff satisfies LOCAL_QUORUM—hints do NOT count as quorum acks; only ConsistencyLevel.ANY accepts a hint as a write success.
Avoid trap: Disabling scheduled nodetool repair because hinted handoff and read repair are enabled, leaving cold keys permanently inconsistent and tombstones unpropagated.
When to reach for it: High-availability AP/tunable-consistency clusters (e.g., Cassandra with RF=3, CL=LOCAL_ONE or LOCAL_QUORUM) where brief node restarts (5–30 minutes) must not stall writes.
When to reach for it: Geo-distributed or multi-AZ deployments experiencing transient cross-AZ packet loss where coordinators can buffer hints locally until peers recover.

putItTogether.title: Putting Hinted Handoff Repair Together
putItTogether.summary: Hinted handoff preserves write availability during brief outages (minutes to a few hours), not durability guarantees; you still need read repair and scheduled anti-entropy repair to prevent zombie data and silent entropy.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Hinted Handoff Repair before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Writes continue with zero client errors at p99 = 6.2 ms. Once the patched node rejoins via Gossip, coordinators throttle hint replay at hinted_handoff_throttle_in_kb (1024 KB/s per node), draining the 8-minute backlog in ~11 minutes without triggering full-range Merkle-tree repairs.
